Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do the major tech companies like Google and Facebook take it upon themselves to become so involved in politics?
Answer: Actually, they'd really rather be left out of politics, but they don't have a choice. Politics is bad for business. No matter what you do, half the country will hate it. Companies want the support of politicians, to influence policy in their favor, and occasionally they need to use their public voice to shift opinions on matters that are very important to them. But they do not want to be visibly involved in politics if they have a choice. But Facebook and Google don't have a choice. Their products are inherently political. They are forced to make choices with political implications. Some examples: *Pro-Nazi material is in fact illegal in some countries, but not the US. Please don't argue in the comments about which decisions these companies have made. The point is that they have to make a choice, and there will always be many people who wish they had made it differently.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why don't MNCs hire people with gaps in their resumes?
Answer: We do. It's definitely a yellow flag, but there are lots of good explanations. They include: By far the most common bad explanation is that the person got fired or quit with no plan, and couldn't get hired again for a while. An average performer with a few years in the industry should generally be able to get another job of similar caliber within a few months by networking with former colleagues. Quitting without a plan shows a lack of foresight or rash decision making. Yet I see that quite frequently. I tend to be more forgiving about it for more junior employees, but it's still not a great sign.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you had the choice to hire a person from Harvard with a 3.5 GPA or a person from a state school with a 4.0 GPA, who would you hire?
Answer: Assuming this is a new grad who majored in Computer Science, I'd strongly prefer the state school grad. 4.0 requires consistent perfection. It's guaranteed that that person has a great work ethic and at least decent intelligence. On the other hand, Harvard has significant grade inflation, so a 3.5 is only a mediocre GPA. Getting into Harvard demonstrates good intelligence and that the kid once worked hard. But I knew many students at Dartmouth who had only worked hard in high school because their parents pushed them. They had no strong work ethic of their own. The 3.5 Harvard grad could be a great hire. But I'm confident the state school kid would be.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is big tech like Google and Twitter banning some speech the same as the book burnings in previous times?
Answer: There have been a few different types of book burnings. In many cases, the government or a mob came to your house and took your books by force. Big tech is nothing like that. If you choose not to associate with them, they'll leave you alone. Sometimes people buy books they don't like in order to burn them, as a protest or to take copies out of circulation. On the internet, copies are free. One could argue that removing videos from YouTube, for example, is a form of protest. But usually protests are designed to capture someone's attention and make a point. When you stage a protest you publicize it. Big tech companies are doing the opposite of that: they make it hard even to know why content was taken down or accounts suspended. Twitter has a thing called “shadow bans", where users' posts are hidden from others but the users themselves aren't notified in any way. That's not what you do when you're making a protest. So no, big tech banning some speech is not equivalent to book burning.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What does it take to become a SVP of Google?
Answer: Exceptional managerial talent and strategic insight coupled with a strong technical skill base. SVPs manage divisions with thousands of people. They are responsible for establishing the culture of that division, which at such a large scale winds up being a big part of the culture of Google as a whole. They set strategies that determine what all those people work on day to day. Those strategies include both business and technical components: what should we build and how should we build it? To get to that point, one must first excel as a lower manager. The prospective SVP needs to build a strong, healthy team culture that attracts and retains top engineers and delivers good business results. There are many ways to do that: some managers are charismatic and personable, some thoughtful and analytical, some are good at asking the right questions and listening to the answers. Google especially emphasizes team culture, compared to somewhere like Amazon that emphasizes results, but you can't make it to SVP without a good dose of both. Technical skills are less important but still necessary. It's impossible to run an engineering team without understanding how the products work and how they're built. However, SVPs aren't there to make technical decisions. Their job is to hire the right people, create a culture that helps them excel, and set a strategy that ensures their efforts achieve the business goal. So it's not critical that they be the best engineer, although it does help. I'm commenting only about SVPs in engineering departments, as that's what my experience is with. However, SVPs manage many different types of worker, not just engineers.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What do you think about Bill Gates' announcement that he is resigning from the Microsoft board?
Answer: Microsoft is in good hands with Satya Nadella. Bill's foundation was the center of his life for a long time, from about 2000–2015, before he returned to Microsoft as an advisor. He came back at Satya's request when Satya was named CEO. Bill probably feels that the company is now strong enough to do fine without him and his business legacy will remain strong, so he can go back to making the world a better place through philanthropy.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why did David Seidman leave Google?
Answer: I got a big promotion, basically. My job at Salesforce is what my boss’s job was at Google. Instead of running part of the detection team, I get to run all of it. The promotion came with a big compensation increase too. It was an opportunity I couldn’t refuse. And it was unlikely I’d get a similar opportunity at Google simply because I had reached the level of management where I needed someone above me in the org chart to leave in order to open up a spot, and it didn’t seem likely any of them were going to. There was nothing at all wrong with my job at Google. I really loved it there and could see myself returning someday, if the circumstances were right. At this stage of my career, there are only a few jobs at the right level of management in the right subject area, so it’s pretty unlikely that one of them will come open at the same time that I am looking for a change myself. But you never know.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Has anyone you've known simply disappeared? Under what circumstances?
Answer: My friend's cousin disappeared, and it was an interesting lesson in media bias. She didn't come home one day. They found her necklace, broken, next to her car, in a nearby park. Her photo was in all the local newspapers: a cute smiling blonde girl in her high school softball uniform, well liked and a good student. Her family held press conferences pleading for whoever took her to let her go. A few weeks later, she did return. But she had not been kidnapped - it had been staged. She had actually run off with her boyfriend against her parents’ wishes. The photo of the cute blonde girl was replaced by a photo of her with dyed black hair, dark goth clothing and a look of defiance. The papers began reporting that the well liked good student had been caught shoplifting and was in trouble at school. She was eventually sentenced to community service for faking the crime. This was the same person. When they wanted to make her look innocent, she looked innocent. When they wanted to make her look guilty, she looked guilty. Think about that next time you read the news.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are people okay with companies like Google or Facebook taking away their privacy?
Answer: Because it's an exchange. You give up your data and you get an awesome service for no cash cost. Most people find that to be a really good deal. Most people think they don't have much to hide and that it's unlikely their data will be misused anyway. I was once told that only about 1% of the American population shares privacy advocates' beliefs. About 30% of people care somewhat about their privacy, and 70% care almost not at all. However, everyone cares about the privacy of their health and financial data and private messages. I heard this from a privacy expert, but I have no other sources, so take it for what it's worth.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why should top-level managers carry out regular progress assessments?
Answer: As an employee, if you weren't doing what the boss wanted, wouldn't you want to know as soon as possible? A good manager wants the same thing. Surprises in a performance review are a bad thing for both people. Of course, the manager does also care about how projects are progressing, because other people care about the outcome. Customers might be waiting for a feature before purchasing, or another team might need to use the thing you're making. If the project is not running on time, they need to be kept informed. Also, if there are problems, the manager can often help. Perhaps a team member isn't pulling their weight, another team is being uncooperative, or the team isn't clear about its priorities. These are all things the manager can and should deal with. But if they don't know how well things are progressing, they can't help.

Question: What are the reasons Indians are highly represented in the boards and CEOs of big corporations in America and the Middle East? (disproportionately to their overall numbers in these countries)
Answer: Because the smartest, best qualified Indians are the ones most able to move to the United States and other countries. Immigrants in general tend to be more successful than native citizens of the country they moved to.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does Google struggle to integrate experienced executives into their engineering teams?
Answer: Google has a very particular management culture. Individual engineers are given a ton of autonomy. Managers have much less control over technical and strategic decisions than at most other companies. Googlers have many job opportunities, so if they don't like what their manager is telling them to do, they can and will go get a job elsewhere. Furthermore, Google's technical infrastructure is unique and complex. Usually the technical expertise an executive has won't directly apply to Google's systems. Yet Google, and Googlers, expects managers to be quite technical. Executives hired from outside often fail to meet this expectation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Does an MBA help you move into engineering management?
Answer: Generally, no. In my experience, engineering managers are hired based on their technical skills, strategic decision-making, mentorship, leadership, and overall ability to get things done through others. The kind of financial and entrepreneurial skills taught in an MBA are not very relevant. Leadership skills are better learned on the job. Also, there is substantial bias against MBAs. The perception is that they are overpaid intellectual lightweights whose only skill is charisma, and that engineers pursue MBAs only when they aren't very good at engineering. An MBA could be useful for an engineer planning to found a company. Otherwise, get a technical Masters degree or just keep working as an engineer. Job experience is the most valuable qualification of all.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is Google "genuinely struggling" with how to deal with employee discontent, according to CEO Sundar Pichai? What makes the employees so unhappy and what should Google do to alleviate this?
Answer: Google has steadily built up mistrust between employees and upper management through a series of apparent cover-ups of bad behavior and direct clashes with employees. These include a project to build a censored search engine for China, a collaboration with the US military, and an apparent sexual harassment payoff to former executive Andy Rubin. The company also fired engineer James Damore after he published an anti-political correctness memo and fired several liberal activists over activity related to leaking. Google is also changing its business substantially in its attempt to compete as a public cloud provider. Working with enterprises requires a very different mindset than working with consumers, which have historically been Google's main customers. The engineering, marketing and sales orgs are all having to change the way they operate, and it's a painful shift for many people. The way Cloud salespeople get paid changed, which is scary for everyone and reduced the size of some people's paychecks. And for all of those efforts, Google's still stuck in 3rd place. So there's a sense of discomfort, fear and failure underlying the direct conflicts over political issues. The first set of problems have two clear solutions. #1, don't do things you wouldn't want your employees to find out about. #2, if you do get caught, provide a full, clear and transparent explanation. To a certain extent they've been limited by legalities, but they've also communicated in an unclear and seemingly untrustworthy way. Whether management was in the right or the wrong, they have mostly responded with a weak rebuttal that neither apologizes nor explains convincingly why the behavior was not bad. The second set of problems are unavoidable as long as Google stays in the cloud business. Its employees will have to learn to work with a different customer base, and to be paid according to their ability to do so. Those who don't want to change are going to be unhappy. There's not much to be done about it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How are the tech workers dealing with a decline in their equities?
Answer: In my experience, most people are grumbling and expect their employer to give large stock grants in this year's compensation cycle. If that doesn't happen there will be a lot of people who change jobs to a company that will pay them their true market value. There are certainly many people who have already done this. I think there's also been a tempering of expectations about how much upside to expect from stock grants. Although people would always have acknowledged that stocks don't always go up, they had certainly gotten used to it. This downturn has brought a little uncertainty back into their thinking.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is the "hack back" bill that is being proposed in Congress a good idea?
Answer: There's a reason the linked article refers to hacking back as “the worst idea in computer security.” It is. Attribution is hard. The defender might hack back at the wrong target. A clever attacker could even attack one organization in a way designed to trick them into “hacking back” at a second victim. Collateral damage is also a problem. Most attacks use a chain of compromised systems to hide the attackers’ tracks. A hack back is likely to damage some of those systems. The attackers will make sure of that. Hack back is vigilante justice for the internet. It sounds good until you're wrongly on the receiving end.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What skills do you need to become a threat detection engineer?
Answer: “Threat detection engineer” isn't an industry standard title. However, it does have meaning. “Threat detection” means trying to catch hackers. It's not a coincidence that my team is named Threat Detection. This role typically involves writing search queries of log data and network traffic to identify attacks. To know what to look for, you'll need a good understanding of all the different types of attack: what the attack is for, how it works, and what traces it leaves behind. You can build this knowledge through self study and/or certifications like OSCP and demonstrate it on the job in an entry level Security Operations Center or Help Desk job. Alternately, you can study computer science in college (undergrad or graduate) and focus on security. “Engineer” means that you will be expected to develop tools and infrastructure, usually with some amount of coding. In addition to writing search queries, you may automate investigations or build new data processing and monitoring systems, for example. To prepare for this, a computer science degree is ideal, but self study, open source work, or a coding boot camp can also prepare you. The usual title of a position with no engineering expectation is “analyst”. A position advertised as “engineer” could just be an analyst position with pretensions, though.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Can I change my gender to increase the odds of getting hired?
Answer: I am assuming you are not actually transgender and are merely speculating about a potential loophole. To legally change your gender requires, at minimum, a sworn statement that the new gender is your sincerely held gender identity. It would be a crime to make such a statement dishonestly. Name changes for purpose of deceit are also illegal in every state I'm familiar with. A legal gender or name change isn't required to use a name and clothes typical of another gender during the job application process. The company will also see your legal name and know that you're transgender, as far as they're concerned. They may discriminate against you on this basis - gender identity isn't protected by law at the US federal level, though it is in some states and cities. On the other hand, they can't legally prefer one gender over another. I've been involved in dozens of interviews and hires, and we have never discussed the applicant's gender. We also don't discuss gender identity. In addition to being illegal, these factors are simply not relevant to job performance. So overall, pretending to be transgender won't help your odds of being hired, might hurt them, and could even be illegal.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do tech companies often have meetings before 8 AM and after 8 PM? How are people productive in this environment?
Answer: In my career, the only times I've had meetings at those hours was to accommodate another time zone or when there was an urgent security incident. I have meetings tonight from 8:30–10 PST with folks in Hyderabad on IST, 12.5 hours offset. 8 am PST is good for US EST and Europe. Very rarely I've had to schedule a meeting at 8 am to get on the calendar of an executive. I've never scheduled a meeting outside of 8–5 except in those two cases, and if someone in my time zone invited me to a meeting outside of 8–5, I'd decline without hesitation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are the Microsoft Patches named with a KB number? Does this mean they are named after knowledge base articles?
Answer: Yes. Each patch has its own Knowledge Base article describing what's in it and how it works. This is also used to uniquely identify each update. You can easily access the KB article by going to https://support.microsoft.com/kb/<the KB number>.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do the CEOs of fortune 500 companies have body guards for their security?
Answer: Yes. My former krav maga instructor used to work as one. Often the bodyguards, also known as “executive protection", are paid for by the company, because the company's stock would lose a ton of value if the executive were assassinated.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can smaller companies attract senior staff?
Answer: Smaller companies can attract good engineers by giving them more responsibility and autonomy than they would get at a bigger company. At Salesforce, I'm responsible for about 3% of the security organization. At a smaller company, I might run 33% of security or even the whole thing. I might be managing the same number of people, but I would be responsible for doing more things and given more discretion in how to do them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Elon Musk correct in reportedly saying that engineering managers should spend their time coding?
Answer: I think it's ideal for engineering managers to spend about 10% of their time coding. The purpose is not to generate useful code but rather to ensure the manager is familiar with the team's technology and code base. If a team member proposes changing a technical dependency or refactoring the code, a manager who has done some hands on engineering will have a better sense of whether the proposal is a good one. The manager will also have a better sense of how different team members have contributed to the code base, which helps with performance reviews. However, this is only really feasible up to about 6 or 7 direct reports. Once a manager has more than that, they generally don't have enough spare time to keep coding. I kept coding until I had 8 direct reports. It might be reasonable for a company to require managers to code a bit as a demonstration of proficiency, as long as most managers have 8 or fewer reports. It would be pretty dumb to require managers to make meaningful code contributions, except at the very smallest companies. If you want more development work to get done, hire more developers. And expecting a manager to deal with 8+ direct reports while still adding features in code is going to lead to crappy code, crappy management, or most likely both. It's not just that time is limited, but also people are more effective at their jobs when they're able to specialize.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do so many people want to remain working remotely and not return to the office?
Answer: Most of my team members who want to stay remote cite the following reasons: They generally don't mind the physical environment at home and are fine with the loss of water cooler socializing. Not everyone wants to remain remote but these are the common reasons for people who do.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How long would it take to work your way up to become a principal engineer at a big tech company?
Answer: The Principal title isn't used uniformly across the industry, but I'll assume it means the level after Senior. At Google this would be level 6, at Microsoft levels 65–67. A very exceptional college grad might start at Google level 4. A promotion to level 5, Senior, might be possible within 1.5 years. A promotion to level 6 might be possible 2 years later, 3.5 years total. The two limitations on growth are that the employee will not immediately be trusted to run higher level projects, and promotion requires demonstrating sustained performance at the next level. This speed of growth would only be possible for an absolute genius with an incredible work ethic and great social skills. I have never seen anyone get to level 6 anywhere close to this speed. A more typical path is to enter at level 3 and get promoted to L4 after 1–2 years. The promotion from 4 to 5 might take 1.5–5 years, although some people never reach level 5. The promotion from 5 to 6 can happen in 3 years, or, for many people, it never happens. So a typical path to Principal might take about 10 years. That is exactly what it took me: I left Microsoft for Google after 10 years and was promoted to Principal in the transfer.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some recent advancements that have been made in the cyber security field that are being implemented now in 2020?
Answer: Much of the security industry's energy has gone into building security tools for the cloud and migrating their own technology there. There isn't a particular achievement that's occurred so much as, “things that worked on regular servers now also work in the cloud”. In my subfield of detection and response, some of the big developments came into the market a few years ago but are just getting widely deployed now. One of them is Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents. These let detection and response teams get almost any data in real time from any system that might be compromised. Another trend is Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR) which automates investigating and responding to alerts of potential compromises. SOAR can automatically do the work of sometimes dozens of analysts, who can now do more sophisticated investigations and projects. A huge development is that we essentially agreed as an industry on a standard list of known attacker techniques, ATT&CK, produced by MITRE. This gives us a standard against which we can measure our prevention and detection measures. It isn't perfect, but it's far better than anything we've had before. We're starting to see 2FA everywhere, which is forcing attackers to use more sophisticated phishing methods. It's only taken 20 years… Another industry trend is purple team, in which red team (offense) and blue team (detection and response) work together to maximize the effectiveness of red team's exercises. Blue team guides red team to attach specific things in specific ways that they want to test, and red team keeps specific notes that are helpful to blue.

Name: David Seidman
Question: I was asked this question at a job interview: “Suppose we hire you and your first job is to fire 20% of people in your department. How do you find out who's doing nothing?” How would you decide who to fire?
Answer: First, I would question why they're hiring someone to do the firing rather than doing it themselves. It might be okay, if the intention is to rebuild a broken organization from scratch, or it might indicate management that won't accept responsibility. I would also be worried about the team's future, and the company's. That said, I'd try to fire the 20% who are performing worst. Usually it's pretty easy to know who the underperformers are. You can look at previous performance reviews, though they can be unreliable. You can look at the projects people are working on, the speed of progress and the quality of output. Any experienced engineering manager should be able to evaluate from scratch how well someone is doing based solely on their work and the way they interact with their teammates. I would have to ignore peer reviews, lest I create a backstabbing culture. However, if I had enough time to judge through observation how the team members view each other, I would take that into account. Even if I think they're wrong, if the team thinks I fired the wrong person, team chemistry will be badly damaged. Generally, though, team members know very well who is performing badly. I also would not consider the impact on the individuals’ personal lives. If you didn't work hard enough to make the cut, that's on you, not me.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do recruiters find underrepresented minority (URM) candidates for job roles?
Answer: The standard ways are attending conferences and networking with organizations aimed at those groups. Those don't really work all that well, in my opinion, because the people who participate in this things are already likely to apply. A newer approach that seems to be working is waiting to get a certain number of resumes, then picking the best candidate, rather than picking the first candidate that meets the minimum qualifications. As a simple matter of statistics, this means you're more likely to get the best candidate who's on the market and also to consider more minority candidates. If there are fewer minority candidates but they're just as good, by collecting more resumes, you're more likely to find a minority candidate who is also the best candidate. And if the best candidate isn't a minority candidate, that's fine too.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How should I handle being asked to do things that are clearly not part of my job description?
Answer: Ask how you'll be rewarded. The answer may very well be, “You'll get to keep your job.” If so, you'll have to decide whether that's a deal you're okay with or if it's time to look for another job. More likely you'll be told to expect a pay raise and/or promotion in the future. The promised reward may or may not actually happen. Again, if you don't get an actual reward for the extra work, you'll have to decide whether you're going to quit over it. In the best case, they are giving you more responsibility because they think you can handle it and want to promote you. Businesses love good workers, and perhaps they believe you are one.

Name: David Seidman
Question: I interviewed with Google but because I am not from the US I didn't get the job but the recruiter didn't reject me. They told me I should reach out if I saw any positions in other countries. Was I rejected?
Answer: It sounds like you did a phone screen, not a full interview. Normally before they bring someone in for full interviews, they'll figure out the visa situation if one is needed. Nobody wants to waste time on interviews if there's little chance the candidate could be hired for legal reasons. It sounds like that's what happened: they were interested in you as a candidate, but determined they probably couldn't get you a visa. Visa processing is very slow right now, so a lot of managers don't want to risk a long delay and high chance of failure (assuming an H1B visa).

Name: David Seidman
Question: When it comes to creating safe and beneficial technological innovations, would you have more trust in a united team of government scientists, or the scientists hired by competing corporations, and why?
Answer: If you want safety, rely on government employees. They won't innovate much of anything, so you won't have to worry about whether it's safe. This isn't anti-government snark, it's about incentives. The Director of Safe Innovations isn't going to get fired for not innovating enough, but definitely will be fired for releasing something unsafe. If you want innovation, look to the private market. Humans innovate profusely without needing any encouragement. Competition drives companies to improve their products year after year. But private companies may not prioritize safety as a result of bankruptcy law: in most countries, a failed company's owners can't be held responsible for the company's debts or even its illegal behavior. When a drug company negligently makes a deadly drug and is eventually sued into oblivion, its investors don't have to give back the dividends they received along the way. Heads I win, tails you lose. One possible fix is to end limited liability and let creditors collect a company's debts from it's investors. This would dramatically reduce the amount of risk taken by private industry, as investors demand verifiable assurances of safety. It would also reduce innovation, because the downside of trying something new would now be larger. The balance between safety and innovation would be set by investors - with their own butts on the line. No system can eliminate all risk. Accidents happen and people make mistakes. But the best we can do is to create a system wherein a well resourced group of people has a strong incentive to find the right balance between safety and innovation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do you know someone is actually intelligent and not just faking it?
Answer: There are many kinds of intelligence. A well rounded intelligent person can teach you something about their field of expertise in 5 minutes, regardless of what you currently know. Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, used to ask interview candidates, “Teach me something I don't know.” They may not always be able to do it in person. Some people are not good verbal communicators or are shy. But they can do it in writing. These people do well in whatever field they're in. They tend to be the ones, like Einstein, who we hold up as geniuses, because their intelligence is easily understandable by others. Other people are problem solvers. You can give them a unique challenge and they will solve it quickly and well, sometimes even beautifully. They may not be able to communicate well about it, which can limit their workplace effectiveness, but they do well in fields like academic mathematics or engineering. You can distinguish them from fakers by asking a hard problem and seeing how fast they solve it. Often they will solve problems incidentally, without even thinking about it. Some people are encyclopedias. They have every fact at their fingertips. They may not be great at coming up with solutions or communicating them, but they do really well in complex and fast moving environments where there isn't time to look things up. Great mechanics often have this ability. “On this model car, between 1998 and 2000, the head gasket was made in Cleveland by WidgetCo, and they used grade 101 rubber which is prone to cracking on cold weather.” Ask them anything factual and they'll know the answer. Some people are incredibly creative. They come up with ideas nobody's ever thought of, or they find ways to make things work that everyone else thought was impossible. Examples include comedians and entrepreneurs. You can't really test this kind of person, because creativity is spontaneous, but they should have a track record you can look at. Some people have incredible empathy. They can almost tell you what you're feeling, and they know what to say to connect emotionally with you. They make great managers and therapists. You can't really test this either unless you're emotionally gifted yourself, and if you are, you'll know.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are big companies having their CEO step down in very high rates in the last three months?
Answer: I've heard rumors of a recession for a long time. Recessions are a crappy time to be a CEO. So my speculation is that those executives are getting out before the storm. Now that coronavirus has struck, there will definitely be a recession, but that wasn't predictable when most of these executives decided to retire. Those announcements are made well after the decisions to retire in order to prepare an orderly transition. This is part of why departing executives get large severance packages - to incent them to stick around for a while when they're already able to retire in luxury.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How long is it reasonable for your current position to keep you from an internal transfer to a new department?
Answer: In my experience in big tech, a 2–3 week transition is standard, and 4 or more is quite uncommon. I believe that at Microsoft managers were not allowed to hold back internal transfers for more than 4 weeks without special approval.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do smaller tech companies survive without being dominated by Big Tech?
Answer: Small tech companies survive because they target markets the bigger companies consider too small or uncertain to bother with. There are many companies providing applications for very specific purposes. For example, I interned for a company that made software to collect and collate data from the sensors in prototype aircraft during testing. This company likely made in the tens of millions of dollars in revenue. At Microsoft I was told that VPs won't even consider a proposal projected to earn less than $100 million, because they already have many proposals worth more than that. Big business is big. There are also ideas that could be big, but probably won't be. There are lots and lots of this kind of idea, far too many for any one company to build or even invest in. Instead, the big companies let startups experiment and then acquire the successful ones.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the best career path for an engineer that doesn't want to manage people?
Answer: Most larger tech companies, and all the giant ones, have a complete career path for non-managers, who are formally called Individual Contributors (ICs). There is no difference in pay between managers and ICs at the same level. ICs at higher levels of seniority are expected to have impact at increasingly large scale. The most senior ICs are expected to have influence across the company or the industry as a whole. A senior IC might work on problems like “design the way text styles will be stored in the file format.” A very senior IC might work on problems like “design the Chrome memory manager" or “figure out how to reduce latency 100x.” Not all companies have this track, so you may need to switch jobs when you get to the point that it matters.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you were an L7 at some company, then joined Google, would you retain the L7 position or does Google reduce it based on their equalization policies?
Answer: A senior position at another company will increase your chances of an interview at Google, and the interview panel will ask questions appropriate for that level. A level 7 equivalent at another large tech company will almost certainly get an interview. However, if an offer is made, the level of the offer will depend mostly on the interview results. Google is notorious for offering people lower level positions than the ones they currently hold. People still take the offers, because of pay, perks and prestige, primarily. The assigned level has nothing to do with race, gender or other demographic attributes or efforts to diversify the workforce. Those things are not considered at all in assigning the level.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why don’t tech companies or data scientist companies have training classes to lead into hiring?
Answer: The ROI isn't there. If you are really good at computers, there's a good chance you'll wind up in the field anyway, even if you have to take out a bunch of loans to do it. The salaries earned by engineers at big tech companies can easily pay off student loans in just a few years. Talented folks who don't go to school can work their way up at other jobs. For the company, there's no need to pay to reason people who would otherwise pay to train themselves. The people who might benefit from a training program are those who lack the confidence or aptitude to make it on their own. Obviously a company doesn't want to train those who have no aptitude. So that means the only people who would pay back the company's investment are those who have aptitude but not confidence. It's really hard to identify these people and distinguish them from those without aptitude and those who would pay for their own training. On top of that, if a company does successfully train someone, that person can quit and take those skills to a competitor. The company can put provisions in place to mitigate that, like requiring the person to pay back the training costs if they leave too quickly. But it's hard to make those provisions tight enough to be useful without being so tight as to be unpalatable or even illegal. That said, companies do have some training programs. These are often targeted at specific demographics that the company believes are likely to have aptitude but not confidence. There are some obvious reasons why people lack confidence: precarious financial situations, poor secondary education, and discrimination, among others. Companies try to target these groups for training. But the programs are usually pretty limited for the reasons given above.
